38 The diagram shows a potential divider connected to a 12 V supply of negligible internal
resistance.
300 Ω
12 V
X
0 –100 Ω
Y
Which range of voltages can be obtained between X and Y?
A
0 to 3 V
B
0 to 4 V
C
0 to 8 V
D
0 to 9 V

hints: Notice that terminals X and Y are connected across only the variable $0-100 \, \Omega$ resistor at the bottom of the series pair.
Recall the potential divider rule for two series resistors: the share of the $12 \, \text{V}$ supply across the lower resistor is proportional to its resistance divided by the total resistance.
Check the two extremes of the slider: set the lower resistance to $0 \, \Omega$ for the minimum, then to $100 \, \Omega$ with total $400 \, \Omega$ for the maximum.
walkthrough: The $300 \, \Omega$ resistor and the $0-100 \, \Omega$ variable resistor are in series across the $12 \, \text{V}$ supply, and $V_{XY}$ is the p.d. across the variable resistor only.
For series resistors the divider rule is $V_{out} = V_{in} \times R_{out}/R_{total}$, so $V_{XY} = 12 \times R_{var}/(300 + R_{var})$ with all resistances in $\Omega$ and voltages in $\text{V}$.
Minimum: when $R_{var} = 0 \, \Omega$, $V_{XY} = 12 \times 0/(300+0) = 0 \, \text{V}$ because there is no resistance to develop a p.d.
Maximum: when $R_{var} = 100 \, \Omega$, total resistance is $300 + 100 = 400 \, \Omega$, so $V_{XY} = 12 \times 100/400$.
This gives $V_{XY} = 12 \times 0.25 = 3.0 \, \text{V}$, so the output can be varied continuously from $0$ to $3 \, \text{V}$.

A.explanation: When the variable resistance is $0 \, \Omega$ the p.d. is $0 \, \text{V}$, and when it is $100 \, \Omega$ the divider gives $12 \times 100/400 = 3 \, \text{V}$.

B.explanation: A value of $4 \, \text{V}$ would need the lower resistance to be one half of the upper $300 \, \Omega$ resistance, but its maximum is only $100 \, \Omega$.

C.explanation: This treats the $300 \, \Omega$ resistor as the output resistor, giving $12 \times 300/400 = 9 \, \text{V}$ incorrectly subtracted from $12 \, \text{V}$.

D.explanation: This is the maximum voltage across the fixed $300 \, \Omega$ resistor, not across the $0-100 \, \Omega$ resistor between X and Y.
